sentences.text: This is an application for grant of regular bail in case FIR No. 447/2024, under Sections 80(2)/85/3(5) BNS, 2023, registered at Police Station Sarai Rohilla.
2. On 06.08.2024, ASI Anil received a PCR call about a woman, Rashida, threatening to consume poison near Pillar No. 181, Sarai Rohilla.
On reaching the spot, police found she had been taken to Aruna Asaf Ali Hospital, where she was later declared dead due to ingestion of an unknown substance.
Inquiry revealed that Rashida had been married to Parvez for about three years and had been harassed by her husband, father-in-law This is a digitally signed order.

Statements from her mother, Farida Begum, and brother, Mohd. Fazil, corroborated consistent dowry-related harassment, prior incidents of violence, and threats from in-laws.
The applicant confessed to frequent quarrels and monetary demands.
Material evidence, including a diary, phone, and suicide notes, were seized.
Further investigation established a pattern of cruelty and dowry demands leading to Rashida's suicide.
Accordingly, a chargesheet was filed against the applicant and co-accused Islamuddin, Tahura, Rumana, Azimuddin, and Saima under Sections 80(2), 85(3)(5) of the BNS 2023.
3. Learned counsel for the applicant submitted that the applicant has been in custody since August 2024, i.e., for over 14 months, and is facing trial under Section 80(2) of the BNS, 2023.

It is further submitted that the deceased committed suicide within seven years of her marriage,
rendering it an unnatural death, and therefore, a presumption under law arises against the husband.
Though PW-3 has turned hostile, his testimony partially supports the prosecution case.
It was further submitted that two public witnesses are yet to be examined, and therefore, at this stage, the applicant does not deserve the concession of bail.

6. Upon consideration of the submissions and material on record, it is evident that the applicant has been in judicial custody since August 2024, and the trial has substantially progressed, with all material witnesses, including the parents and brothers of the deceased, having been examined.
The prosecution's case of dowry-related harassment finds no substantive corroboration in their testimonies.

Except for a limited statement by PW-3, Mohd. Fazil, who only deposed that "his sister was not living happily with Parvez," no specific allegation of dowry demand or cruelty has been attributed to the applicant.

It is further observed that the applicant has already undergone incarceration for over 14 months,
and the trial is likely to take considerable time to conclude.
The investigation is complete, the chargesheet stands filed, and no further custodial interrogation of the applicant is required.

The prosecution's reliance on the presumption arising from the death of the deceased within seven years of marriage is weakened in light of the consistent testimonies of the family members of the deceased denying any dowry demand or cruelty by the applicant.

Moreover, the medical condition of the deceased, as noted in the testimony of PW-1 and PW-6, indicates that she was suffering from tuberculosis, which could have contributed to her deteriorating mental and physical state, thereby diluting the alleged nexus between the applicant's conduct and her death.

9. In Sanjay Chandra v. CBI (2012) 1 SCC 40, the Supreme Court held that the primary object of bail is to secure the accused's presence at trial and not to punish or preventively detain him, as deprivation of liberty before conviction is contrary to the presumption of innocence.
The Court emphasized that pre-trial detention should be justified only by necessity, such as ensuring attendance at trial, and that refusal of bail merely as a form This is a digitally signed order.
The authenticity of the order can be re-verified from Delhi High Court Order Portal by scanning the QR code shown above.
The Order is downloaded from the DHC Server on 09/10/2025 at 22:14:03 of punishment or disapproval of conduct is impermissible.

It further observed that bail discretion must be exercised cautiously, balancing individual liberty with societal interests, and that denial of bail without sufficient cause undermines the very foundation of the criminal justice system.

The relevant paras of the judgment read as under;
"21.
In bail applications, generally, it has been laid down from the earliest times that the object of bail is to secure the appearance of the accused person at his trial by reasonable amount of bail.
The object of bail is neither punitive nor preventative.
Deprivation of liberty must be considered a punishment, unless it is required to ensure that an accused person will stand his trial when called upon.

The courts owe more than verbal respect to the principle that punishment begins after conviction,
and that every man is deemed to be innocent until duly tried and duly found guilty.
22.
From the earliest times, it was appreciated that detention in custody pending completion of trial could be a cause of great hardship.

From time to time, necessity demands that some unconvicted persons should be held in custody pending trial to secure their attendance at the trial but in such cases, "necessity" is the operative test.

In this country, it would be quite contrary to the concept of personal liberty enshrined in the Constitution that any person should be punished in respect of any matter, upon which, he has not been convicted or that in any circumstances, he should be deprived of his liberty upon only the belief that he will tamper with the Parvez vs State Nct Of Delhi on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/165531117/
3 witnesses if left at liberty, save in the most extraordinary circumstances.
23.

sentences.text: Apart from the question of prevention being the object of refusal of bail, one must not lose sight of the fact that any imprisonment before conviction has a substantial punitive content and it would be improper for any court to refuse bail as a mark of disapproval of former conduct whether the accused has been convicted for it or not or to refuse bail to an unconvicted person for the purpose of giving him a taste of imprisonment as a lesson.
25. The provisions of CrPC confer discretionary jurisdiction on criminal courts to grant bail to the accused pending trial or in appeal This is a digitally signed order.
The authenticity of the order can be re-verified from Delhi High Court Order Portal by scanning the QR code shown above.

The Order is downloaded from the DHC Server on 09/10/2025 at 22:14:03 against convictions; since the jurisdiction is discretionary, it has to be exercised with great care and caution by balancing the valuable right of liberty of an individual and the interest of the society in general.

In our view, the reasoning adopted by the learned District Judge, which is affirmed by the High Court, in our opinion, is a denial of the whole basis of our system of law and normal rule of bail system.
It transcends respect for the requirement that a man shall be considered innocent until he is found guilty.

If such power is recognised, then it may lead to chaotic situation and would jeopardise the personal liberty of an individual."
10.

At the stage of grant of bail, the Court is not to meticulously examine and appreciate the evidentiary value of testimonies of the witnesses, but at the same time, it cannot be ignored that the family members of the deceased have not supported the prosecution case.

11. Hence, keeping in view the overall facts and circumstances coupled with the fact that most of the material witnesses have already been examined and, therefore, there is hardly any possibility of threatening or influencing the witnesses, the Court is of the view that no useful purpose would be served by continued detention of the applicant.

c) the applicant shall remain available on the address, to be given to the IO and shall not leave the State of Delhi/NCT without the permission of the learned Trial Court;
d) In case of change of residential addresses and/or mobile number, the applicant shall intimate the same to the Investigating Officer/ Court concerned by way of an affidavit; and e) Upon being released, applicant shall share his mobile number to the IO and shall keep the same operational all the times.
12. In view of the above, the petition alongwith any pending application, if any, stand disposed of.
13. Nothing stated herein shall tantamount to be an expression in the merits of the case.
14. A copy of this order be sent to Jail Superintendent for necessary compliance.
